To keep instruments warm under the surgical lights
To pass items quickly and safely without contamination
explanation: Organized, visible instruments improve workflow and help maintain the sterile field.

stem: A sterile team member turns away from the sterile field. What is the concern?
options: Their back may brush against a non-sterile surface
The field may no longer be under visual control
The surgeon may lose track of the instrument count
Air currents may carry bacteria onto the gown front
explanation: Sterile fields must remain in view and controlled by sterile personnel.

stem: Which action is appropriate when a sterile instrument is passed to a surgeon?
options: Pass it with the tip pointed toward the surgeon
Pass it closed and unlocked so it can be opened
Firmly, into the surgeon's palm, ready to use
Set it on the patient so the surgeon can pick it up
explanation: Controlled passing protects the sterile field and reduces injury risk.

stem: What is the role of the scrub technician during an operation?
options: Monitor anesthesia and record the patient's vitals
Keep the field sterile and hand off instruments
Open supplies and bring items from outside the field
Prepare the patient's skin before the drapes are placed
explanation: The scrub technician works within the sterile field to support the procedure.

stem: Which factor can impair steam sterilization?
options: Packs placed on their edges in the chamber
Instruments left open and unlocked in the pack
Indicator tape placed on the outside of the pack
Trapped air in the chamber or pack
explanation: Air pockets interfere with steam contact and heat transfer.

stem: Why should sterilized packs cool before handling or storage?
options: To let the chemical indicator finish changing color
To prevent the instruments from becoming dull
To let any remaining steam finish sterilizing
To avoid condensation and maintain package integrity
explanation: Handling hot packs can cause condensation and compromise the sterile barrier.

stem: What are typical conditions for a gravity steam sterilization cycle?
options: About 121 °C (250 °F) at about 15 psi
About 100 °C (212 °F) at normal room pressure
About 160 °C (320 °F) of dry heat at 0 psi
About 55 °C (131 °F) with ethylene oxide gas
explanation: Pressurized steam at 121 °C kills spores in a typical 15–30 minute exposure. Prevacuum cycles use about 132 °C for shorter times.

stem: A procedure requires a sterile implant. What should be confirmed before opening it?
options: Package integrity, indicators and expiration date
The implant's size only, since sterility is assured
That it was stored with the other sterile packs
Only the manufacturer's name and catalog number
explanation: Implant traceability and package integrity are essential before use.

stem: In brachygnathism (an overshot jaw), which statement is true?
options: The maxilla is shorter than the mandible
The jaws are equal but the incisors are rotated
The mandible is shorter than the maxilla
Only the canine teeth are displaced lingually
explanation: Brachygnathism is mandibular distoclusion (Class 2). The opposite, a long mandible or short maxilla, is mesioclusion (Class 3), common in brachycephalic breeds.

stem: Which structure anchors the tooth within the alveolar socket?
options: Gingival sulcus
Cementoenamel junction
Periodontal ligament
Alveolar mucosa
explanation: The periodontal ligament connects the tooth root to alveolar bone.

stem: What is the purpose of dental probing around each tooth?
options: Measure how far the gingiva has receded only
Remove calculus from below the gumline
Assess periodontal pocket depth and attachment
Test each tooth for mobility in its socket
explanation: Probing evaluates gingival sulcus depth and periodontal attachment.

stem: Why is a complete oral examination performed under anesthesia in many patients?
options: It lets the team skip intraoral radiographs for most patients
It is required only when extractions are already planned
It lets the technician polish without scaling below the gumline
It permits systematic assessment and treatment while reducing movement risk
explanation: Anesthesia allows thorough examination and instrumentation with controlled patient movement and airway protection.

stem: Which area is most likely to be missed by visual examination alone?
options: The lingual surfaces of the incisors
The cusp tips of the premolars
The buccal surface of the canines
Subgingival tooth and root structures
explanation: Subgingival and root disease may not be apparent without probing and imaging.

stem: A dental radiograph shows a widened periodontal ligament space. What is an appropriate interpretation?
options: Possible periodontal or periapical disease to evaluate
It shows the tooth is vital and needs no further workup
It is a normal finding in every adult dog and cat
It confirms a tooth resorption lesion of the crown
explanation: A widened ligament space can be associated with pathology and must be interpreted with the full study.

stem: What is the main purpose of scaling?
options: Remove plaque and calculus from tooth surfaces
Smooth the enamel after polishing is finished
Remove stain and tartar from the gingiva only
Shorten the crown height of overgrown teeth
explanation: Scaling removes deposits from supragingival and subgingival tooth surfaces.

stem: Why is polishing performed after scaling?
options: Strengthen the enamel by adding fluoride to it
Remove the calculus that scaling missed below the gum
Smooth the scratches left by scaling
Seal the dentinal tubules after an extraction
explanation: Polishing smooths surfaces after scaling; it does not sterilize or replace other assessment.

stem: Which instrument is commonly used for dental extraction of a tooth root fragment?
options: Periosteal elevator
Curette
Root tip pick forceps
Dental elevator
explanation: Elevators are used to loosen periodontal ligament attachments during extraction.

stem: Which tooth is the carnassial tooth of the dog's upper jaw?
options: Maxillary fourth premolar (108/208)
Maxillary first molar (109/209)
Maxillary third premolar (107/207)
Maxillary canine (104/204)
explanation: The upper fourth premolar and lower first molar are the carnassial teeth. The upper fourth premolar is a common site of slab fractures and tooth root abscesses.

stem: Why should a dental scaler tip remain in motion when applied to a tooth?
options: To reduce heat buildup and local tissue injury
To push calculus deeper into the gingival sulcus
To keep water from spraying the operator's face
To let the tip cut faster through the enamel
explanation: Continuous movement and appropriate technique reduce heat concentration.

stem: Which finding may support a diagnosis of tooth resorption in a cat?
options: Generalized yellow staining on the canine crowns
Smooth gingival recession with no defect present
A focal defect in the crown or root
Heavy calculus on the upper fourth premolars
explanation: Feline tooth resorption can produce visible lesions and radiographic changes.

stem: What is the purpose of an occlusal examination?
options: Measure the depth of each periodontal pocket
Check each tooth for mobility and fractures
Count the number of teeth that are present
Assess how the teeth meet when the jaws close
explanation: Occlusion describes the relationship between upper and lower teeth.

stem: How many roots does a dog's maxillary fourth premolar have?
options: One
Two
Three
Four
explanation: It has two mesial roots and one distal root. Each root must be sectioned and elevated separately during extraction.

stem: Which nerve block is used to desensitize mandibular teeth on one side?
options: Middle mental nerve block
Infraorbital nerve block
Caudal maxillary nerve block
Inferior alveolar nerve block
explanation: An inferior alveolar block desensitizes mandibular teeth and associated tissues on that side.

stem: Which nerve block commonly desensitizes maxillary teeth rostral to the maxillary foramen?
options: Inferior alveolar nerve block
Femoral nerve block
Sciatic nerve block
Infraorbital nerve block
explanation: The infraorbital nerve supplies rostral maxillary structures, depending on anatomy and technique.

stem: What should be included in a dental chart?
options: A summary of the overall oral health grade
Only the teeth that were extracted that day
Tooth-by-tooth findings and procedures performed
The anesthesia drugs and monitoring values
explanation: Dental charts document findings and treatment at the individual tooth level.

stem: Why should dental radiographs be obtained before and after an extraction when indicated?
options: To see roots before and confirm removal after
To confirm the tooth was vital before extraction
To decide how much local anesthetic to give
To show the client before and after photos
explanation: Radiographs help identify root anatomy and assess completeness of extraction.

stem: Which tissue covers the visible crown of a healthy tooth?
options: Enamel
Cementum
Pulp
Periodontal ligament
explanation: Enamel covers the crown; cementum covers the root.

stem: What is the primary concern when a dental instrument is damaged or has a rough surface?
options: It may scratch the enamel and change its color
It will dull more quickly and need sharpening
It may cause the scaler to overheat the water
It may injure tissue or impair effective treatment
explanation: Damaged instruments can cause trauma and should be removed from service for repair or replacement.

stem: Which tooth numbering system records each tooth using a three-digit identifier?
options: Universal tooth numbering system
Anatomic quadrant system
Modified Triadan system
Palmer notation system
explanation: The Modified Triadan system assigns three-digit numbers to individual teeth.

stem: A dental patient is recovering from anesthesia. Which observation is important?
options: Jaw tone and the ability to chew food
A clear airway and return of the swallow reflex
Polishing paste removed from the lips
Return of the palpebral reflex only
explanation: Airway and recovery monitoring remain important after dental procedures.

stem: Which tube additive is commonly used for a CBC?
options: EDTA
Sodium citrate
Plain fluoride only
Formalin
explanation: EDTA preserves cellular components for hematology when used at the correct ratio.

stem: Which additive is commonly used for coagulation testing?
options: EDTA
Lithium heparin
Formalin
Sodium citrate
explanation: Citrate binds calcium reversibly and is used for coagulation assays at the specified blood-to-additive ratio.

stem: Why must a citrate tube be filled to the indicated volume?
options: The blood-to-citrate ratio affects clotting results
Overfilling the tube clots the sample before testing
The tube's vacuum is needed to separate plasma
Underfilling the tube causes hemolysis in the sample
explanation: Underfilling changes the citrate ratio and can produce unreliable coagulation results.

stem: What is serum?
options: Urine after centrifugation
The fluid portion of clotted blood
The cellular portion of anticoagulated blood
Whole blood with EDTA
explanation: Serum is the liquid remaining after blood has clotted and cells have been removed.

stem: What is plasma?
options: The liquid left after a blood sample has clotted
The packed cells at the bottom after spinning
The buffy coat layer and the platelets above it
The fluid portion of anticoagulated blood
explanation: Plasma is obtained from anticoagulated blood and contains clotting proteins.

stem: A sample is lipemic. What does this describe?
options: Excess lipid in the serum or plasma
Red blood cells ruptured in the sample
A high bilirubin level that turns plasma yellow
Bacterial overgrowth in a sample left too long
explanation: Lipemia is turbidity from elevated lipid content and may interfere with some assays.

stem: What is a buffy coat?
options: The red cell layer packed at the bottom of the tube
White cells and platelets above the red cells
The clear plasma layer at the top of the spun tube
The clotted fibrin strands that settle after spinning
explanation: The buffy coat lies between plasma and packed erythrocytes in a spun hematocrit tube.

stem: What is the purpose of a reticulocyte count?
options: Count the platelets and measure their function
Measure the total hemoglobin of mature cells
Show whether the bone marrow is responding
Detect blood parasites inside the red cells
explanation: Reticulocytes are immature erythrocytes; their number helps evaluate marrow response to anemia.

stem: Which blood cell type is primarily involved in hemostasis?
options: Platelet
Erythrocyte
Lymphocyte
Eosinophil
explanation: Platelets participate in primary hemostasis and clot formation.

stem: A urine sample has a specific gravity of 1.045. What does specific gravity primarily estimate?
options: The amount of protein in the urine
Urine concentration relative to water
The urine's acidity or alkalinity
The number of cells in the sediment
explanation: Specific gravity reflects the concentration of dissolved substances in urine.

stem: Which urine test pad detects heme-associated peroxidase activity?
options: Protein pad
pH pad
Blood pad
Ketone pad
explanation: The reagent pad detects heme activity and may react with intact cells, hemoglobin, or myoglobin.

stem: Why should urine sediment be examined after centrifugation and resuspension?
options: To measure the urine's specific gravity accurately
To look for cells, casts and crystals
To check the urine's pH and protein level
To estimate the amount of glucose present
explanation: Urine sediment microscopy identifies formed elements that dipstick analysis cannot characterize.

stem: Which finding is most consistent with bacteriuria on urine sediment examination?
options: A few squamous cells in a free-catch sample
Bacteria seen in a sample left out for hours
A positive leukocyte pad on a dog's dipstick
Bacteria observed in a properly collected sample
explanation: Microscopic bacteria may support bacteriuria, but collection method and clinical context matter.

stem: What is the purpose of a fecal flotation?
options: Detect blood in the stool from bleeding ulcers
Identify protozoal trophozoites by their motion
Measure digestion of fat and starch
Float parasite eggs and oocysts to the surface
explanation: Flotation concentrates many parasite ova and oocysts for microscopic examination.

stem: A fecal sample for parasite testing is delayed. What should the technician do?
options: Freeze it until it can be run in the clinic
Leave it at room temperature until it is mailed
Add saline to keep it moist until shipping
Refrigerate it and ship as the lab directs
explanation: Specimen preservation requirements vary by test, so laboratory instructions should be followed.

stem: Why should a blood smear be prepared promptly after collection?
options: To avoid storage changes in cell shape
To keep the platelets from clumping in the tube
To stop the sample from clotting in the EDTA tube
To prevent the smear from drying out before staining
explanation: Delayed smear preparation can alter cellular morphology and distribution.

stem: Which stain is commonly used for routine blood-smear evaluation?
options: Gram stain
Wright-Giemsa-type stain
New methylene blue stain
Acid-fast stain
explanation: Romanowsky-type stains such as Wright-Giemsa are used for blood-cell morphology.

stem: A packed cell volume is measured after centrifugation. What is being quantified?
options: The proportion of blood made up of white cells
The total protein concentration in the plasma
The number of red cells per microliter of blood
The proportion of blood volume occupied by erythrocytes
explanation: PCV estimates the fraction of whole blood made up of packed red cells.

stem: A plasma sample appears pink after centrifugation. What is a likely cause?
options: Icterus
Leukocytosis
Hemolysis
Lipemia
explanation: Free hemoglobin can discolor plasma pink to red after red-cell rupture.

stem: A plasma sample appears yellow. What is a possible cause?
options: High urine specific gravity
Increased bilirubin
Hemolysis
Thrombocytopenia
explanation: Icterus causes yellow discoloration from bilirubin.

stem: Why should a sample be labeled at collection rather than later?
options: To record the exact time the sample was spun
To let the laboratory choose the correct tests
To show the client that the sample was taken
To make sure it matches the right patient
explanation: Immediate labeling prevents mix-ups and preserves specimen traceability.

stem: Which information is important on an outside laboratory submission?
options: The patient's name and the client's phone number
The tests requested and the clinic billing code
Patient ID, sample type, tests and history
The specimen type and the time it was shipped
explanation: Complete submission information supports accurate processing and interpretation.

stem: A chemistry analyzer produces a control result outside the accepted range. What should the technician do?
options: Rerun the control until it falls in range, then report
Hold patient results and troubleshoot the analyzer
Report patient results with a note about the control
Adjust the patient results by the control's error
explanation: Out-of-range quality controls indicate the run may not be reliable.

stem: What is the purpose of calibration on an analyzer?
options: Check that results fall within the reference range
Compare one patient's results with its last values
Test the analyzer's reagents for contamination
Relate instrument response to known reference values
explanation: Calibration establishes the instrument’s measurement relationship to known standards.

stem: Why should laboratory pipettes be maintained and checked?
options: Pipettes that are not cleaned can spread infection
Damaged pipettes can break and cause injury
Accurate volume delivery is essential for reliable results
Pipettes must be sterile for culture samples
explanation: Pipette accuracy and function directly affect test measurements.

stem: Which organism type is identified by a Gram stain’s reaction and morphology?
options: Helminth eggs only
Red blood cells only
Serum proteins
Bacteria
explanation: Gram staining helps classify bacteria by cell-wall reaction and morphology.

stem: What is the primary purpose of culturing a specimen?
options: Identify parasites and their eggs from a fecal sample
Measure how many white cells are in the specimen
Stain the cells so they can be seen on cytology
Grow and identify organisms and test susceptibility
explanation: Culture allows microbial growth and identification; susceptibility testing can guide treatment selection.

stem: Why should a swab for culture be collected before antimicrobial therapy when feasible and directed?
options: Antimicrobials can change the bacteria's Gram stain
Prior treatment makes the sample clot in the tube
Prior treatment may reduce organism recovery
Treatment changes how fast the culture can be read
explanation: Antimicrobials can suppress microbial growth and reduce culture yield.

stem: Which sample is generally best for a blood culture?
options: Blood from an existing IV catheter, drawn after flushing
A single sample of clotted blood in a red-top tube
Blood collected in an EDTA tube for a CBC as well
Blood drawn aseptically into culture bottles
explanation: Blood culture requires aseptic collection and the appropriate culture medium.

stem: A cytology slide is thick and heavily smeared. What may be impaired?
options: The staining time needed
Cell detail
The slide's labeling
The sample's cell count
explanation: Thick, crushed preparations can obscure cell morphology and diagnostic features.

stem: What is the purpose of an air-dried cytology smear?
options: Kill any bacteria present before staining the slide
Preserve cell shape for staining
Make cells stick to the slide so they can be fixed
Increase the number of cells in each field
explanation: Proper drying helps retain cell detail for routine cytologic staining.

stem: What is a typical normal PCV range for an adult dog?
options: About 37–55%
About 15–25%
About 25–30%
About 60–75%
explanation: Adult dogs are roughly 37–55%, cats about 30–45%. Exact reference ranges depend on the laboratory or analyzer.

stem: Which white blood cell is usually the most numerous in a healthy dog?
options: Lymphocyte
Neutrophil
Monocyte
Eosinophil
explanation: Mature neutrophils make up most of the canine and feline differential. In cattle, lymphocytes usually predominate.

stem: A dog arrives with a painful limb. What is the safest initial handling approach?
options: Muzzle the dog right away and lift it by the injured limb
Assess pain and behavior, then use low-stress restraint
Let the owner hold the limb while you examine it closely
Sedate the dog before any assessment of its behavior
explanation: Assessing pain and behavior first helps select safe handling and protect the patient and team.

stem: A cat is hiding in the back of its carrier. What should the technician try first?
options: Tip the carrier upright and let the cat slide out on its own
Keep things quiet and use the carrier or a towel
Reach in quickly and scruff the cat before it can react
Leave the carrier door open in the busy treatment room
explanation: Quiet handling and familiar carrier support reduce fear and improve safety.

stem: A dog shows repeated lip licking, yawning, and avoidance during restraint. What may these behaviors indicate?
options: A desire to play
Stress or discomfort
Normal anesthetic recovery only
Hypoglycemia in every case
explanation: These may be stress signals and should prompt reassessment of the handling plan.

stem: The FVRCP vaccine protects cats against which diseases?
options: Feline leukemia, rabies and chlamydia
Panleukopenia, herpesvirus and calicivirus
Feline immunodeficiency virus and calicivirus
Panleukopenia, feline leukemia and ringworm
explanation: FVRCP covers feline viral rhinotracheitis (herpesvirus-1), calicivirus and panleukopenia. With rabies, these are core vaccines for cats.

stem: A patient is recumbent and cannot reposition itself. Why should its position be changed as directed?
options: To reduce prolonged pressure and support ventilation and comfort
To speed recovery from anesthesia in all recumbent patients
To let the patient drain urine on its own more easily
To keep the IV catheter from becoming kinked or blocked
explanation: Repositioning reduces pressure injury risk and may support comfort and respiratory function.

stem: Which finding should be monitored distal to a limb bandage?
options: Heart rate, respiratory rate, and temperature
Toe pad color and nail length only
The bandage's outer layer for dirt and odor
Swelling, temperature, color, and circulation
explanation: Distal limb checks help identify bandage constriction or impaired circulation.

stem: A patient’s toes become cool and swollen below a bandage. What is the best action?
options: Loosen the outer tape and recheck the toes in an hour
Tell the veterinarian right away; the bandage may be too tight
Elevate the limb and apply ice over the bandage
Add more padding over the toes and keep monitoring
explanation: Cool, swollen digits may indicate impaired circulation and require prompt attention.

stem: What does capillary refill time assess in a basic perfusion check?
options: How long the gums stay pale after pressure is applied
How quickly the jugular vein fills after occlusion
Time for color to return to blanched mucous membrane
The time for the skin to flatten after a skin tent
explanation: Capillary refill time is a quick indicator of peripheral perfusion when interpreted with other findings.

stem: Why should vital signs be recorded with the time of measurement?
options: Times are needed only for patients in intensive care
The time determines which staff member is paid
Trends and timing support clinical interpretation
Vitals without a time can be added to any record
explanation: Time-stamped observations allow the team to evaluate changes over time.

stem: Which information should be included in a nursing note?
options: Objective observations, interventions, and patient response
Only the treatments that were given and their times
Opinions about the owner's care at home
A summary of the diagnosis and the prognosis
explanation: Clear notes document what was observed, done, and how the patient responded.

stem: Which canine vaccine is considered noncore (lifestyle-based)?
options: Canine distemper virus
Bordetella bronchiseptica
Canine parvovirus
Canine adenovirus-2
explanation: Distemper, parvovirus, adenovirus-2 and rabies are core. Bordetella is given based on exposure risk, such as boarding or daycare.

stem: Why should water intake be monitored in a patient with a prescribed fluid-balance plan?
options: Water intake replaces the need to measure urine
Drinking more water always means kidney failure
It is needed only for patients on oral medications
It contributes to total fluid intake and helps assess trends
explanation: Oral water intake is part of overall fluid balance and may affect clinical evaluation.

stem: A urinary collection bag is attached to a catheterized patient. Where should it generally be positioned?
options: Above the bladder so urine flow can be seen
Level with the patient's head to prevent backflow
Below the level of the bladder
On the kennel floor beside the patient's bedding
explanation: Keeping the collection bag below the bladder supports drainage and helps prevent backflow.

stem: Why should a urinary catheter drainage system remain closed when possible?
options: To keep urine output easier to measure each hour
To prevent the catheter from slipping out of place
To reduce contamination and ascending infection risk
To keep the patient from licking at the catheter
explanation: Maintaining a closed system limits contamination.

stem: What should be assessed when monitoring urine output?
options: Color of the urine only, once a day
Volume, appearance, and changes over time
Total volume at discharge only
Specific gravity only, every hour
explanation: Urine volume and characteristics can help assess renal and fluid status.

stem: Which tick is the main vector of Lyme disease in dogs?
options: Ixodes (black-legged or deer tick)
Dermacentor (American dog tick)
Rhipicephalus (brown dog tick)
Amblyomma (lone star tick)
explanation: Ixodes scapularis and Ixodes pacificus transmit Borrelia burgdorferi. Dermacentor is associated with Rocky Mountain spotted fever and tick paralysis.

stem: Which action is appropriate when cleaning a wound for a prescribed treatment?
options: Use dilute chlorhexidine, which is right for every wound
Scrub the wound until it bleeds to remove all debris
Use hydrogen peroxide, which promotes wound healing
Use the solution and technique specified in the treatment plan
explanation: Wound care must follow the prescribed plan and avoid tissue-damaging products or excessive trauma.

stem: Which animal is the definitive host of Toxoplasma gondii?
options: The dog
The pig
The rodent
The cat
explanation: Only cats shed oocysts in their feces. Other animals and people are intermediate hosts, which is why pregnant women are told not to clean litter boxes.

stem: What is the purpose of a Robert Jones bandage?
options: Immobilize a shoulder after luxation
Keep a hind limb from bearing weight
Provide rigid fixation of a femoral fracture
Provide support and padding to a limb
explanation: A Robert Jones bandage is a bulky padded bandage used for limb support and swelling control.

stem: A patient has a pressure sore. Which nursing action is appropriate?
options: Massage the area to bring blood to the sore
Cover it with a tight dressing to protect it
Keep the patient on the same side so it heals
Relieve pressure and follow the wound-care plan
explanation: Pressure relief and a prescribed wound plan are key to preventing progression.

stem: Which position may help support breathing in a dyspneic patient if tolerated?
options: Dorsal recumbency to open the chest fully
Lateral recumbency with the neck flexed down
Standing with the patient's head lowered
Sternal, with the head and neck extended
explanation: Sternal positioning and an open airway may reduce respiratory effort in some patients; avoid unnecessary stress.

stem: A patient is suspected of having a contagious disease. What is the best immediate infection-control step?
options: Move it to isolation and use isolation precautions
Keep it in the main ward but mark its kennel
Move it once its diagnosis has been confirmed
Treat it first so it can go home sooner
explanation: Isolation and appropriate precautions help limit transmission.

stem: What is the correct direction for patient flow in an isolation setting when possible?
options: Bring all patients into the isolation area
Care for healthy patients before isolated patients
Care for isolated patients first, then all healthy patients without changing PPE
Move randomly between rooms
explanation: Healthy-to-isolation workflow reduces the chance of carrying pathogens to susceptible patients.

stem: Why is a long preanesthetic fast unnecessary in rabbits?
options: Rabbits digest food in under an hour
Rabbits are resistant to all anesthetic drugs
Rabbits store food in their cheek pouches
Rabbits can't vomit, and fasting risks gut stasis
explanation: Rabbits can't vomit, so regurgitation is rarely a concern. Withholding food can trigger GI stasis, so food is withheld only briefly, if at all.

stem: Which practice is appropriate for disinfecting a kennel?
options: Spray disinfectant over the debris and rinse right away
Mix bleach with a cleaner for a stronger effect
Use any disinfectant, since contact time doesn't matter
Remove debris, then disinfect for the full contact time
explanation: Organic material can reduce disinfectant effectiveness; contact time and label directions matter.

stem: A new puppy has an unknown vaccination history. What infection-control approach is prudent while awaiting evaluation?
options: Keep it apart from other patients until evaluated
House it with other puppies so it can socialize
Vaccinate it and then allow it in common areas
Keep it with adult dogs that are fully vaccinated
explanation: Unknown vaccination status warrants precautions to reduce exposure risk.

stem: Which item is most important when collecting a history from a client?
options: The pet's breed, color, and age only
Onset, duration, progression and prior treatment
The client's opinion on the diagnosis
What the pet eats and its favorite toy
explanation: A structured history helps the veterinarian understand the complaint and timeline.

stem: Which nutrient must guinea pigs get in their diet every day?
options: Vitamin C
Vitamin D
Vitamin K
Vitamin B12
explanation: Like people, guinea pigs can't make vitamin C. Deficiency causes scurvy: lameness, bleeding gums and poor coat.

stem: Which restraint method is appropriate for a fractious cat when safe and authorized?
options: Scruff and stretch the cat to hold it still
Towel wrap with a trained assistant
Hold it on its back with its legs extended
Hold it by the front legs and the scruff
explanation: Appropriate towel restraint can improve safety while minimizing stress.

stem: A patient becomes increasingly agitated during restraint. What should the team do?
options: Add another person and hold it more firmly
Finish the procedure quickly before it worsens
Release it in the room so it can calm down
Pause, lower stimulation and change the approach
explanation: Escalating distress raises injury risk; reassessment may allow a safer plan.

stem: Which location is commonly used to palpate a dog’s femoral pulse?
options: Tail tip
Medial thigh
Dorsal paw
Lateral neck only
explanation: The femoral artery is palpated on the medial aspect of the thigh.

stem: Which finding should be reported during a routine nursing assessment?
options: New pale mucous membranes
A familiar coat pattern
The patient’s name tag color
A normal relaxed posture
explanation: Pale mucous membranes can indicate poor perfusion or anemia and merit veterinary assessment.

stem: An intact female ferret that stays in heat for a long time is at risk of which condition?
options: Hyperadrenocorticism (Cushing's)
Estrogen toxicity (aplastic anemia)
Insulinoma (hypoglycemia)
Hypercalcemia of malignancy
explanation: Ferrets are induced ovulators. Prolonged estrus keeps estrogen high and can cause life-threatening aplastic anemia, so spaying or hormonal treatment is recommended.

stem: Which measurement should be recorded using a consistent method when tracking body weight?
options: Weight on the same calibrated scale when feasible
Weight on whichever scale is free at the time
Weight estimated from body condition score
Weight taken from the owner's report at home
explanation: Consistent weighing methods improve comparison of serial measurements.

stem: Why should the same scale be used for serial weights when practical?
options: It measures body fat more accurately
It is required for all controlled drugs
It reduces variation between measurements
It keeps the scale from losing calibration
explanation: Using the same calibrated scale improves trend reliability.

stem: A patient’s body condition score is high. What does the score generally describe?
options: Body fat
Muscle mass and strength
Height and length of the body
Daily calorie needs
explanation: Body condition scoring estimates adiposity and should be considered with weight and clinical findings.

stem: Which approach is appropriate when feeding a patient with a prescribed diet?
options: Check the patient, diet and amount before feeding
Feed whatever diet is on hand if the patient is hungry
Mix the prescribed diet with the clinic's regular food
Feed twice the amount so it eats enough overnight
explanation: Diet and amount should match the treatment plan to support safe care.

stem: Why must a bird's chest not be compressed during restraint?
options: Birds need body wall movement to breathe
Birds' ribs are filled with fluid
Birds breathe only through their skin
Compression stops the bird's heart reflexively
explanation: Birds move air through their air sacs by moving the keel and body wall. Holding the chest too tightly can suffocate them.

stem: A tube-fed patient coughs during feeding. What should the technician do?
options: Slow the rate and continue while watching closely
Stop the feeding and promptly notify the veterinarian
Flush the tube with water and then keep feeding
Sit the patient up and finish the feeding faster
explanation: Coughing may indicate aspiration or tube-related complications; stop and assess.

stem: Why should a patient’s bedding be kept clean and dry?
options: To protect the skin and keep the patient comfortable
To reduce how often the patient needs turning
To keep the patient from chewing the bedding
To make cleaning the kennel faster at discharge
explanation: Clean, dry bedding supports skin integrity and patient comfort.

stem: A patient has diarrhea in its kennel. Which action is appropriate?
options: Leave it until the end of the shift to save PPE
Hose the kennel with the patient still inside
Note the stool, clean it up and use isolation precautions
Remove the stool and spray the area without gloves
explanation: Stool quality can be clinically useful and cleanup should limit contamination.

stem: What is an appropriate way to reduce the risk of zoonotic exposure?
options: Hand hygiene and PPE suited to the hazard
Wash hands only after handling sick patients
Wear gloves only when blood is visible
Use the same gloves between patients in one ward
explanation: PPE and hand hygiene are core measures for reducing zoonotic transmission.

stem: Why do hospitalized reptiles need a temperature gradient in their enclosure?
options: They rely on outside heat to regulate body temperature
They overheat because they sweat poorly
Heat is needed only to keep their skin from shedding
A gradient prevents them from becoming dehydrated
explanation: Reptiles rely on outside heat for metabolism, digestion and immune function. A warm side and cool side lets them choose their temperature, the preferred optimal temperature zone.

stem: What is the purpose of a fecal sample collection container label?
options: Tell the laboratory which test to run first
Match the sample to the right patient and time
Record how much stool the patient passed
Show the client that the sample was collected
explanation: Accurate labeling ensures the specimen is traceable to the correct patient.

stem: A patient has a peripheral IV catheter. Which site finding is concerning?
options: A small amount of blood under the dressing
A dressing that is clean and dry
Mild redness only when it is flushed
Swelling, pain, heat, or fluid leakage
explanation: These findings can indicate infiltration, phlebitis, or other catheter complications.

stem: In which stage of the estrous cycle will a bitch accept the male?
options: Proestrus
Estrus
Diestrus
Anestrus
explanation: During proestrus she attracts males but refuses them. In estrus she is receptive and ovulates. Diestrus follows, then anestrus.

stem: Why should an IV catheter be flushed only as directed?
options: Frequent flushing raises the patient's blood pressure
Flushing replaces the need to change the dressing
To check patency without over-flushing
Flushing dissolves clots that form in the vein
explanation: Flush volume and solution must follow the prescribed protocol and catheter type.

stem: A patient is receiving oxygen by flow-by. What should be monitored?
options: Only the oxygen flow rate, once per shift
Only the patient's temperature every 4 hours
Patient response and oxygen setup
Only the humidifier water level each hour
explanation: Oxygen support requires observation of both patient response and delivery method.

stem: A patient is wearing an Elizabethan collar. What is its primary purpose?
options: Keep the patient's head warm after surgery
Help the patient eat and drink more easily
Prevent licking, chewing or scratching
Hold an oxygen mask in place for therapy
explanation: The collar limits access to wounds or devices when properly fitted.

stem: What is an appropriate check of an Elizabethan collar?
options: Fit it tightly so the patient can't slip it off at all
Remove it at night so the patient can sleep
Cut it short so the patient can reach its food
That it fits securely and the patient can eat and breathe
explanation: Correct fit protects the treatment site while allowing normal breathing and swallowing.

stem: A patient is trembling in a cool recovery area. What should the technician do?
options: Take its temperature and warm it safely
Place a hot water bottle against its body at once
Wrap it in heavy blankets and leave it to rest
Increase the room heat and recheck at the next round
explanation: Trembling may reflect hypothermia or other conditions; assess before applying controlled warming.

stem: Why should warming devices be used cautiously in recumbent patients?
options: They may cause thermal injury if the patient cannot move away
They can raise blood glucose in diabetic patients
They interfere with ECG and pulse oximeter readings
They can cause dehydration in long-term patients
explanation: Patients unable to reposition are vulnerable to burns from concentrated heat.

stem: A patient has a seizure. What is the safest immediate action?
options: Place a towel in its mouth to protect the tongue
Hold its limbs firmly until the movements stop
Pick it up and carry it to the treatment table
Clear nearby hazards, time it and get the veterinarian
explanation: Protecting the patient and recording duration help guide emergency care; do not place hands in the mouth.

stem: What should be noted after a seizure ends?
options: The color of the patient's gums during the event
The food and water intake for the day before
The patient's temperature before the seizure
Length, movements, recovery and any repeats
explanation: Detailed observation supports clinical evaluation and seizure management.

stem: What is the average gestation length in the dog?
options: About 42 days
About 90 days
About 114 days
About 63 days
explanation: Dogs average 63 days from ovulation (range about 58–68 days from breeding). Cats are similar, about 63–65 days. 114 days is the sow.

stem: Which technique supports accurate respiratory-rate measurement?
options: Count breaths while the patient is restrained
Watch breathing right after a walk outside
Count the breaths for 5 seconds and multiply
Count breaths before handling the patient
explanation: A calm observation can reduce stress-related changes in respiratory rate.

stem: A patient is scheduled for a treatment that requires fasting. What should the technician verify?
options: That the patient hasn't eaten since admission
That water was removed at the same time as food
The prescribed fasting instructions and timing
That the patient fasted for at least 24 hours
explanation: Fasting instructions are patient- and procedure-specific and should be verified.

stem: Which action helps prevent medication administration to the wrong patient?
options: Check the patient's ID at the kennel
Read the name on the patient's kennel location
Recognize the patient by its breed and color
Ask the client to confirm the patient's cage
explanation: Multiple identifiers reduce wrong-patient errors.

stem: A treatment sheet is missing a route for a medication. What should the technician do?
options: Skip the dose without telling anyone
Clarify the order before administration
Choose the usual route
Use the route from another patient’s chart
explanation: An incomplete order should be clarified rather than interpreted independently.

stem: Why should a patient’s response after a treatment be documented?
options: It is needed only for controlled substances
It shows whether the treatment helped or harmed
It replaces the need for a written order
It confirms that the treatment was billed
explanation: Response documentation supports treatment evaluation and continuity of care.

stem: A patient with suspected contagious diarrhea needs a sample collected. What is important?
options: Wear PPE and keep the sample contained
Collect it in the lobby to keep wards clean
Use the same gloves for the next patient
Carry it uncovered to the lab right away
explanation: Containment, PPE, and clean transport reduce pathogen spread.

stem: Which mite is the most common cause of ear mites in cats and dogs?
options: Sarcoptes scabiei
Demodex canis
Otodectes cynotis
Cheyletiella yasguri
explanation: Otodectes lives in the ear canal and causes dark, coffee-ground debris. Sarcoptes causes scabies, Demodex lives in follicles and Cheyletiella is walking dandruff.

stem: A patient’s appetite improves after treatment. What should the technician do?
options: Increase the amount fed without asking
Stop monitoring since the patient is eating
Record intake and report the improvement
Switch to its home diet at the next meal
explanation: Documenting response helps the team evaluate progress without overinterpreting one sign.

stem: What is the purpose of a clean recovery kennel?
options: Keep the patient awake until it is fully recovered
Keep it away from the treatment area to reduce noise
Let it recover without monitoring in a quiet room
A safe, clean, comfortable place to wake up
explanation: A prepared recovery space supports hygiene and safe observation.

stem: A patient is recovering from anesthesia and has an unsecured endotracheal tube. What is the concern?
options: It will make the patient wake up too quickly
Airway obstruction or injury if the tube is mishandled
It can cause the patient to become hypothermic
It may cause the cuff to deflate on its own
explanation: Airway devices require careful monitoring and removal at the appropriate recovery stage by trained staff.

stem: Pets become infected with the tapeworm Dipylidium caninum by:
options: Swallowing infected fleas while grooming
Eating raw beef or pork
Drinking water contaminated with oocysts
Being bitten by an infected mosquito
explanation: Fleas are the intermediate host. Treating the tapeworm without controlling fleas leads to reinfection.

stem: A patient has a suspected fracture. How should the limb be handled during transport?
options: Let the patient walk if it can bear weight
Keep the limb still and support it
Splint the limb tightly before any assessment
Carry it by the scruff to avoid touching the limb
explanation: Limiting movement reduces pain and risk of further injury.

stem: Why should a patient’s kennel card and medical record be checked together?
options: To confirm the patient's breed and color
To decide which patient to treat first
To make sure the instructions are for this patient
To copy the instructions into the kennel card
explanation: Cross-checking the record and kennel information helps prevent identification and treatment errors.

stem: A patient's temperature is 39 °C. What is this in Fahrenheit?
What is an important nursing consideration for a patient with a pressure-sensitive eye condition?
options: Avoid any pressure on the eye or neck
Hold the head down so tears can drain away
Apply firm pressure to the eyelid to close it
Use a neck lead to keep the head still
explanation: Pressure on the globe can be harmful in some ocular conditions.

stem: A patient is positioned for a lateral abdominal radiograph. Where should the marker be placed?
options: Over the area being evaluated, so it is easy to find
On the patient's skin, taped over the abdomen
On the image receptor side, outside the anatomy of interest
On the table outside the collimated beam
explanation: A visible marker should identify orientation without obscuring diagnostic anatomy.

stem: Why is collimation used in radiography?
options: Limit the primary beam to the area of interest
Increase the beam's energy to improve penetration
Reduce image contrast for soft tissue structures
Make the exposure time shorter for moving patients
explanation: Collimation reduces irradiated volume and scatter while focusing the image on the region needed.

stem: Which three principles reduce occupational radiation exposure?
options: Short exposure, close distance, and a thin apron
More time, more distance, and no apron needed
Minimize time, maximize distance, and use shielding
Lead gloves only, held close to the primary beam
explanation: Time, distance, and shielding are the core radiation-protection principles.

stem: A radiograph is blurred. Which cause is most likely?
options: Correct marker placement
Proper collimation
Motion during exposure
Accurate positioning
explanation: Patient movement during exposure causes motion blur.

stem: What is the purpose of using sandbags or foam positioning aids?
options: Increase the image's contrast for soft tissue
Raise the patient closer to the X-ray tube
Hold the position so staff stay out of the beam
Replace the need for collimation of the beam
explanation: Positioning aids help stabilize the patient and reduce the need for personnel to hold it.

stem: Which personnel should remain in the room during an exposure?
options: Everyone on the team, if each one wears an apron
Only essential, protected staff
Only staff under 18 years old who are not pregnant
The client, so the pet stays calm during exposure
explanation: Limiting personnel in the room reduces unnecessary radiation exposure.

stem: Why should hands not be placed in the primary x-ray beam?
options: Lead gloves block all radiation in the primary beam
Hands in the beam blur the image of the patient
The beam can expose tissue to ionizing radiation
Gloves make it harder to keep the patient still
explanation: Hands are radiosensitive and should not be exposed to the primary beam.

stem: What is the purpose of a lead apron and thyroid shield?
options: Shield staff completely from the primary beam
Reduce occupational exposure to scattered radiation
Improve image contrast by absorbing scatter
Measure each staff member's total exposure
explanation: Protective apparel attenuates scatter but does not replace other radiation-safety practices.

stem: What does a personal dosimeter monitor?
options: Scatter radiation from the patient during one exposure
The X-ray tube's output for quality control
Cumulative occupational radiation exposure
The dose the patient receives from each image
explanation: Dosimeters track an individual’s occupational exposure over time.

stem: An image is too light because too few photons reached the detector. Which adjustment may improve receptor exposure under protocol?
options: Increase mAs
Decrease mAs
Remove the grid in every case
Increase motion
explanation: mAs controls photon quantity; exposure adjustments must follow the imaging protocol.

stem: What does kVp primarily influence in radiography?
options: The number of X-rays produced
Beam energy and image penetration
The sharpness of the image
The size of the focal spot
explanation: kVp affects photon energy and penetration, as well as image contrast.

stem: A radiograph is overexposed. Which parameter primarily controls the quantity of x-ray photons?
options: Collimation
Focal-film distance only
mAs
kVp only
explanation: mAs controls the number of photons produced during the exposure.

stem: Why should the patient be positioned symmetrically for a ventrodorsal view?
options: Make the exposure time shorter for the study
Reduce rotation and improve image interpretation
Allow a lower kVp setting to be used
Keep the patient from moving during exposure
explanation: Symmetrical positioning reduces rotation-related distortion.

stem: What does ultrasound gel do?
options: Cool the probe so it can be used for longer exams
Remove air between the probe and the skin
Act as a contrast agent that highlights blood flow
Clean the skin so the probe stays sterile
explanation: Gel improves acoustic coupling by removing air at the interface.

stem: Which ultrasound artifact appears as repeated parallel echoes from repeated reflections?
options: Acoustic shadowing
Hemolysis
Collimation
Reverberation
explanation: Reverberation results from sound reflecting repeatedly between strong interfaces.

stem: What causes acoustic shadowing behind a structure?
options: Sound passing through fluid with no echoes
The sound beam reflecting back and forth
A mismatch between the gel and the skin
Bone or gas blocking the sound beam
explanation: Highly attenuating or reflective structures reduce sound transmission to deeper tissues.

stem: Why may a fluid-filled structure appear anechoic on ultrasound?
options: Fluid reflects all the sound back to the probe
Fluid transmits sound with few internal echoes
The gain is set too high for that depth
Fluid absorbs the sound before it returns
explanation: Simple fluid generally produces few internal echoes and appears dark.

stem: Which contrast agent is preferred when a gastrointestinal perforation is suspected?
options: Barium sulfate
Iodinated contrast
Air (negative contrast) only
Gadolinium
explanation: Barium that leaks into the abdomen causes severe granulomatous peritonitis. Water-soluble iodinated contrast is absorbed if it leaks.

stem: Which imaging modality uses ionizing radiation to create cross-sectional images using x-rays?
options: Ultrasonography
Magnetic resonance imaging
Endoscopy
Computed tomography
explanation: CT uses x-rays and computer reconstruction to form cross-sectional images.

stem: Which modality uses a strong magnetic field and radiofrequency pulses rather than ionizing radiation?
options: Computed tomography
Fluoroscopy
Nuclear scintigraphy
MRI
explanation: MRI relies on magnetic fields and radiofrequency signals, not ionizing x-rays.

stem: Why is accurate patient and view labeling important?
options: It improves the image's contrast and detail
It is needed only for images sent to specialists
It links the image to the correct patient and orientation
It allows the image to be stored in the right folder
explanation: Correct labeling is essential for identification and interpretation.

stem: Before anesthetic induction, which check is essential?
options: Verify the oxygen source, machine function, breathing circuit, and monitoring equipment
Confirm the vaporizer is full; the other checks can wait until after induction
Check the patient's fasting time and weight; the machine is checked weekly
Turn on the monitors after intubation so the alarms don't sound early
explanation: Equipment checks help ensure reliable oxygen and anesthetic delivery before induction.

stem: What is the purpose of a preanesthetic evaluation?
options: Identify patient factors that may affect anesthetic risk and planning
Choose the cheapest drug protocol that will be safe for the patient
Confirm the client has paid the deposit for the anesthetic procedure
Decide whether the patient needs a breathing circuit at all
explanation: Preanesthetic assessment helps the veterinarian plan for patient-specific risks.

stem: A breathing circuit fails a leak test. What should happen?
options: Turn up the oxygen flow so the leak doesn't matter
Use it for short procedures and fix it afterward
Locate and correct the leak before using the circuit
Switch to a mask so the leak won't affect the patient
explanation: Leaks can impair ventilation and anesthetic delivery, so the circuit must be corrected first.

stem: What does a reservoir bag allow the team to do?
options: Measure the exact tidal volume of each breath during anesthesia
Warm and humidify the gases before they reach the patient
Store extra oxygen in case the cylinder runs low during a case
Observe and assist ventilation and assess breathing-system response
explanation: The reservoir bag helps visualize breathing and permits manual ventilation when appropriate.

stem: What is the primary purpose of an oxygen flush valve?
options: Fill the reservoir bag with anesthetic gas quickly
Measure the patient's inspired oxygen concentration
Deliver high-flow oxygen while bypassing the vaporizer
Flush exhaled CO2 out of the absorbent canister
explanation: The flush valve provides high-flow oxygen and should be used with awareness of pressure risks.

stem: Why can careless use of the oxygen flush valve be hazardous to a patient on a breathing circuit?
options: It dilutes the inhalant so the patient may wake up
It can deliver high pressure and volume rapidly
It drops the oxygen level in the circuit to zero
It cools the gases and causes hypothermia quickly
explanation: High flow can cause excessive circuit pressure, especially with a closed airway or small patient.

stem: What does a capnogram display?
options: Oxygen saturation of hemoglobin in arterial blood
The concentration of inhalant in the exhaled gas
Carbon dioxide concentration over the respiratory cycle
Respiratory rate and tidal volume over time
explanation: Capnography displays exhaled carbon dioxide throughout the respiratory cycle.

stem: A capnogram suddenly becomes flat during anesthesia. What should the technician do first?
options: Increase the vaporizer setting until the trace returns
Replace the capnograph sampling line and keep going
Assume the sampling line is kinked and keep monitoring
Check the patient, airway, circuit and sample line
explanation: A flat tracing may reflect apnea, disconnection, obstruction, or sampling failure and requires immediate assessment.

stem: What does pulse oximetry estimate?
options: Carbon dioxide in the exhaled breath
The amount of oxygen dissolved in plasma
Peripheral arterial oxygen saturation
The partial pressure of arterial oxygen
explanation: Pulse oximetry estimates hemoglobin oxygen saturation in pulsatile peripheral blood.

stem: A pulse oximeter reading is erratic during movement. What is an appropriate response?
options: Record the lowest reading as the patient's true value
Move the probe to the tail and stop checking the patient
Check probe position and signal quality while assessing the patient
Turn the alarm off until the patient stops moving
explanation: Movement and poor signal can cause artifact; verify the reading and assess the patient.

stem: What does an ECG monitor during anesthesia?
options: Electrical cardiac activity and rhythm
Cardiac output and stroke volume
Blood pressure and perfusion
The strength of each heartbeat
explanation: ECG shows electrical activity and helps identify rhythm disturbances.

stem: A monitor displays an unexpected ECG rhythm. What should the technician do?
options: Record it as normal sinus rhythm, since artifacts are common
Check the patient and leads, then tell the veterinarian
Give atropine, since most new rhythms are bradyarrhythmias
Remove the ECG leads and rely on the pulse oximeter instead
explanation: Artifact is possible, so patient assessment and lead verification are important.

stem: Which method can provide a noninvasive blood-pressure estimate?
options: Doppler or oscillometric monitoring
Pulse oximetry and capnography
Arterial catheter only
Esophageal stethoscope
explanation: Doppler and oscillometric devices can estimate blood pressure noninvasively.

stem: Why should the blood-pressure cuff be sized appropriately?
options: Cuff size changes the patient’s blood type
A larger cuff always gives the most accurate result
Cuff size only affects temperature
Incorrect cuff size can distort the measurement
explanation: Cuff width and fit influence measurement accuracy.

stem: Why is midazolam often combined with ketamine for induction?
options: It speeds the metabolism of ketamine
It adds muscle relaxation to offset ketamine's muscle rigidity
It reverses ketamine's effect on the eyes
It provides most of the analgesia in the combination
explanation: Ketamine alone causes muscle rigidity. A benzodiazepine adds relaxation and smooths induction and recovery.

stem: Why are anesthetized patients at risk of hypothermia?
options: Inhalants raise the patient's metabolic rate and heat loss
Oxygen given during anesthesia cools the body directly
Patients sweat more heavily while under general anesthesia
Anesthesia impairs thermoregulation and heat conservation
explanation: Anesthesia and patient preparation can reduce heat production and promote heat loss.

stem: Which warming method is safest for a recumbent patient when approved?
options: An electric heating pad on high, directly under the patient
A controlled warming device with regular skin checks
Hot water bottles placed against the patient's skin
A heat lamp aimed close to the patient's chest
explanation: Controlled warming with frequent checks reduces thermal-injury risk.

stem: Alfaxalone is best described as:
options: An alpha-2 agonist sedative
An opioid analgesic
A neurosteroid anesthetic
An inhalant anesthetic
explanation: Alfaxalone is a neurosteroid that acts on GABA-A receptors. It can be given IV or IM for sedation and induction.

stem: What is the purpose of preoxygenation when indicated?
options: Lower the dose of induction drug needed
Increase oxygen reserves before induction
Prevent the patient from vomiting during induction
Reduce the patient's heart rate before intubation
explanation: Preoxygenation increases oxygen available during the induction period.

stem: Which action helps confirm appropriate endotracheal tube placement?
options: Inflate the cuff and listen for gurgling over the stomach
Confirm that the patient coughs once the tube is placed
Check that the tube moves freely in and out of the mouth
Chest movement and CO2 on the capnograph
explanation: Multiple checks help confirm tracheal placement and ongoing ventilation.

stem: The endotracheal tube cuff is inflated. What should be avoided?
options: Excessive cuff pressure
A cuff inflated just enough to seal
Checking the seal at 20 cm H2O
Tying the tube to the upper jaw
explanation: Excessive cuff pressure can injure tracheal mucosa.

stem: Why is an endotracheal tube secured after placement?
options: To keep the cuff from deflating during the procedure
To prevent the patient from swallowing the tube
To keep the tube from kinking against the teeth
To reduce the risk of displacement or accidental extubation
explanation: Securement helps maintain airway access during positioning and surgery.

stem: A patient’s breathing circuit disconnects. What is the immediate concern?
options: Rising blood pressure from excess inhalant
A sudden increase in the patient's heart rate
Loss of ventilation and anesthetic delivery
Inhalant pooling in the patient's lungs
explanation: Disconnection can rapidly compromise ventilation and anesthetic depth.

stem: What is an appropriate response to a suspected circuit disconnection?
options: Reconnect it, check breathing and alert the veterinarian
Turn up the vaporizer to make up for the lost gas, then reconnect
Wait for the patient to start breathing on its own again
Switch the patient to mask delivery until the end of the case
explanation: Restoring the breathing circuit and assessing the patient are immediate priorities.

stem: What does a scavenging system do?
options: Remove waste anesthetic gases from the work area
Recycle exhaled oxygen back to the patient
Remove carbon dioxide from the breathing circuit
Warm the gases before they reach the patient
explanation: Scavenging captures or removes waste anesthetic gases to reduce occupational exposure.

stem: A waste-gas scavenging hose is disconnected. What should happen?
options: Turn the vaporizer down and finish the case as is
Open a window to vent the gas until the case ends
Continue the case, since exposure is minimal
Reconnect it to limit staff exposure
explanation: A disconnected scavenging system can release waste gases into the room.

stem: Why is the anesthetic vaporizer kept upright during use?
options: Tilting it can damage the oxygen flowmeter
It is calibrated to work upright
It must be level for the scavenger to work
An upright vaporizer prevents overheating
explanation: Many vaporizers depend on correct orientation for accurate anesthetic delivery.

stem: What should be checked when filling an anesthetic vaporizer?
options: The brand of oxygen tank and its pressure
The color of the vaporizer and the circuit
The time of the last machine service only
Correct agent, fill level, and spill prevention
explanation: Correct agent and safe filling prevent wrong-agent use and exposure.

stem: What is a common consequence of inadequate ventilation during anesthesia?
options: Carbon dioxide retention
Low urine concentration only
Improved oxygen saturation in all cases
Increased body temperature in every patient
explanation: Hypoventilation can cause hypercapnia and requires assessment and correction.

stem: A patient’s end-tidal CO2 rises progressively. What should the technician do?
options: Increase the oxygen flow and wait for the next reading
Assess ventilation, equipment, and patient status; alert the veterinarian
Turn the vaporizer up so the patient breathes more slowly
Change the capnograph line, since the reading is likely wrong
explanation: A rising trend can indicate hypoventilation or other issues and merits prompt assessment.

stem: Why should anesthetic depth be assessed using multiple indicators?
options: Monitors are unreliable during most anesthetic procedures
Depth is set by the vaporizer alone in most patients
Reflexes disappear in a fixed order in all species
No single sign reliably describes the entire patient state
explanation: Combining clinical signs and monitoring provides a more complete assessment.

stem: A patient becomes bradycardic under anesthesia. What is an appropriate technician response?
options: Give atropine right away, since bradycardia is always dangerous
Turn the vaporizer up, since bradycardia means pain
Check perfusion and depth, then tell the veterinarian
Record it and keep going, since bradycardia is expected
explanation: Bradycardia must be interpreted with patient status and anesthetic context.

stem: What does an esophageal stethoscope help monitor?
options: Heart and respiratory sounds
Blood glucose
Urine output
Anesthetic vaporizer concentration
explanation: An esophageal stethoscope permits ongoing auscultation during anesthesia.

stem: Which position can reduce pressure on dependent tissues during a long procedure?
options: Appropriate padding and planned repositioning when feasible
Tie all four limbs tightly so the patient can't shift
Place the patient on a bare metal table to stay cool
Keep the patient in one position for the whole case
explanation: Padding and position management help prevent pressure and nerve injury.

stem: Why should the eyes be protected during general anesthesia when indicated?
options: Anesthesia raises pressure inside the eye
Bright surgical lights damage the retina
Inhalant gases irritate the conjunctiva
Fewer blinks dry out the cornea
explanation: Anesthetized patients may have reduced tear distribution and blinking.

stem: Which signs are typical of stage II of anesthesia?
options: Ventromedial eye rotation and steady breathing
Fixed dilated pupils and apnea
Normal voluntary movement and awareness
Involuntary excitement and paddling
explanation: Stage II is the excitement or delirium stage. Smooth induction moves the patient through it quickly to stage III, the surgical plane.

stem: Why should anesthetic records include time-stamped monitoring values?
options: They replace the surgical report in the record
They are needed only if a complication happens
They help the clinic bill for anesthesia time
They show trends and support continuity and review
explanation: Time-stamped data help the team identify changes and evaluate the anesthetic course.

stem: A patient begins swallowing during recovery. What should the technician consider?
options: It may be nearly ready for extubation
The patient needs more inhalant to stay asleep
The patient is having a seizure during recovery
The cuff should be inflated further at this time
explanation: Protective reflexes inform recovery, but extubation timing is assessed by trained staff.

stem: Why should oxygen continue during recovery when prescribed?
options: Oxygen speeds the elimination of all injectable drugs
It may still breathe poorly as drugs wear off
Oxygen is needed to keep the patient asleep longer
Oxygen prevents the patient from becoming painful
explanation: Recovery patients may have residual respiratory depression or other support needs.

stem: Which sign requires close attention during anesthetic recovery?
options: Shivering as the patient warms up
Obstructed or noisy breathing
Slow, deep, regular breaths
A slight rise in heart rate
explanation: Airway obstruction can deteriorate quickly and requires prompt assessment.

stem: What should be done if a pulse-oximeter probe loses its signal?
options: Record the last good reading until the signal returns
Check the probe, the site and the patient
Turn off the monitor to stop the alarm and recheck later
Increase the oxygen flow until the signal comes back
explanation: Probe and signal problems must be resolved before interpreting saturation.

stem: A patient has a sudden drop in end-tidal CO2 and weak pulses. What is the priority?
options: Check circulation and breathing; call the veterinarian
Increase the vaporizer to deepen the patient
Check the capnograph line first, since it's likely kinked
Reduce oxygen flow and recheck in five minutes
explanation: The combination can indicate a serious change in perfusion or ventilation and requires immediate assessment.

stem: Which item is important to record when a monitoring device is repositioned?
options: Only the name of the person who moved it
The time and relevant patient or equipment change
Nothing, since the device was moved, not the patient
The new reading only, without the time
explanation: Documenting changes helps interpret readings and maintain a useful anesthetic record.

stem: Why should a rebreathing system’s carbon dioxide absorbent be checked?
options: Exhausted absorbent releases inhalant into the room
Old absorbent blocks oxygen flow to the patient
Exhausted absorbent raises the vaporizer output
Exhausted absorbent can allow CO2 rebreathing
explanation: Absorbent removes carbon dioxide in a rebreathing circuit and must be monitored.

stem: Which clue may indicate exhausted CO2 absorbent?
options: The reservoir bag fills more slowly than usual
A color change or rising inspired CO2
The granules become soft and turn pure white
The oxygen flowmeter reading drops suddenly
explanation: Color indicators and inspired CO2 trends can signal absorbent exhaustion; follow the product protocol.

stem: What is the purpose of an anesthetic induction agent?
options: Provide pain relief for the whole procedure
Keep the patient asleep without an inhalant
Relax the muscles so no analgesia is needed
Get the patient ready for intubation
explanation: Induction agents facilitate transition to general anesthesia under the veterinarian’s plan.

stem: Why is analgesia considered as part of an anesthetic plan?
options: To replace the need for an inhalant anesthetic
To make the patient recover more quickly
To address nociception and improve patient comfort
To lower the cost of the anesthetic protocol
explanation: Pain control is a distinct and important part of perioperative planning.

stem: A patient arrives with severe respiratory distress. Which assessment has the highest immediate priority?
options: Circulation and perfusion
Airway and breathing
Temperature and hydration
Neurologic status
explanation: Airway and breathing are immediate priorities in an unstable patient.

stem: A collapsed patient is unresponsive and not breathing normally. What should the team do?
options: Place an IV catheter first, then start compressions
Call a code and start CPR
Give two rescue breaths and recheck in a minute
Take a full history from the owner before starting
explanation: Unresponsiveness with abnormal breathing requires immediate resuscitation response.

stem: During CPR, what helps improve compression effectiveness?
options: Allow full chest recoil and minimize interruptions
Pause every cycle to check for a pulse
Compress slowly and deeply about 60 times a minute
Lean on the chest between each compression
explanation: Effective compressions require recoil and minimal pauses.

stem: A patient has uncontrolled external bleeding. What is an appropriate initial action while summoning help?
options: Apply direct pressure with clean gauze
Apply a tourniquet above the wound right away
Remove each soaked gauze and replace it with new
Lavage the wound to see where the bleeding is
explanation: Direct pressure can help control external hemorrhage while the team prepares further care.

stem: A patient is suspected of shock. Which combination is concerning?
options: Weak pulses, pale mucous membranes, and altered mentation
Bounding pulses, red gums, and a slow heart rate
Normal pulses, pink gums, and mild panting
Strong pulses, dry gums, and normal mentation
explanation: These findings may indicate poor perfusion and require urgent evaluation.

stem: What is the purpose of triage?
options: See patients in the order they arrive at the desk
Rank patients by how urgent they are
Assign each patient to the next available doctor
Decide which tests each patient will need first
explanation: Triage identifies who needs the most immediate assessment and intervention.

stem: A patient with suspected spinal injury needs transport. What should the team do?
options: Let the patient walk to see which legs are affected
Carry it in your arms, supporting its chest only
Check reflexes by flexing the neck before moving it
Minimize spinal movement and coordinate stabilization
explanation: Limiting movement reduces risk of worsening injury.

stem: A patient is seizing in the treatment area. What is the safest action?
options: Hold the head and limbs firmly so it can't hurt itself
Clear hazards, time it and call for help
Place a towel in its mouth to protect the tongue
Move it to a quiet kennel right away and recheck later
explanation: Protecting the patient and documenting duration support safe emergency care.

stem: A patient has suspected heat illness. What is an appropriate first response?
options: Wrap it in wet towels and let it rest until it cools
Remove it from heat and start cooling
Put it in an ice bath until it stops panting
Give cold water by mouth and recheck in an hour
explanation: Prompt controlled cooling and veterinary assessment are essential; avoid unmonitored extremes.

stem: Why should cooling stop when directed before the patient becomes hypothermic?
options: Overcooling can worsen instability
It prevents the thermometer from working
Cooling does not affect body temperature
It increases heat illness
explanation: Active cooling must be monitored to avoid overshooting into hypothermia.

stem: A patient may have ingested a toxic substance. What information is most useful to obtain?
options: Substance, amount, time, route, and patient details
The pet's diet, vaccines, and last meal
The product's price and where it was bought
The pet's weight and the client's address
explanation: Exposure details guide risk assessment and treatment decisions.

stem: A cat suddenly can't use its hind legs, cries in pain, and the hind feet are cold with no femoral pulses. What is most likely?
options: Intervertebral disc herniation
Hip luxation on both sides
Aortic thromboembolism
Tick paralysis
explanation: A saddle thrombus blocks blood to the hind limbs, causing pain, cold pale pads and absent pulses. It is usually linked to heart disease such as hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

stem: A patient with trauma has a suspected open fracture. What is appropriate while awaiting veterinary treatment?
options: Rinse and scrub the wound, then replace the bone
Cover it with a sterile dressing and keep it still
Leave it uncovered so the vet can see it right away
Apply a tight splint over the exposed bone
explanation: A clean covering and movement restriction help protect the wound until treatment.

stem: Which sign may indicate worsening neurologic status?
options: Declining responsiveness
Normal purposeful movement
Improved orientation
Stable posture
explanation: A decline in mentation can signal neurologic or systemic deterioration.

stem: Grapes and raisins can cause which problem in dogs?
options: Hemolytic anemia
Liver failure from hypoglycemia
Acute kidney injury
Methemoglobinemia
explanation: The toxic dose varies and is unpredictable, so any ingestion is treated with decontamination and fluids. Tartaric acid is the suspected toxin.

stem: Why is oxygen delivery checked during emergency support?
options: Oxygen tubing loses pressure after a few hours of use
A disconnected or empty source can make the therapy ineffective
Patients can become dependent on oxygen therapy
Oxygen flow rate must match the patient's heart rate
explanation: The equipment and oxygen source must be functioning for oxygen therapy to help.

stem: A patient with suspected anaphylaxis develops facial swelling and collapse. What should the technician do?
options: Give an antihistamine and recheck in 30 minutes
Place the patient in a quiet kennel to calm it
Call the veterinarian and start emergency care
Apply cold packs to the face and watch for change
explanation: Anaphylaxis can rapidly compromise circulation and airway and is an emergency.

stem: A patient is receiving blood products and develops hives and vomiting. What should happen?
options: Slow the rate and continue while watching for fever
Give an antiemetic and continue the transfusion
Stop the transfusion and tell the veterinarian
Finish the unit quickly before more signs develop
explanation: New signs during transfusion may indicate a reaction and require immediate veterinary assessment.

stem: Why is patient reassessment repeated after an emergency intervention?
options: To decide when the patient can go home
To record vitals for billing and inventory
To confirm the first assessment was right
To see whether it worked or the patient worsened
explanation: Repeated reassessment shows whether the intervention is working and whether further action is needed.

stem: A patient has a deep puncture wound. Why is veterinary evaluation important even if the opening looks small?
options: Small punctures need only a topical antibiotic
Deeper tissue damage and contamination may be hidden
Puncture wounds rarely cause serious infection
They heal faster if the opening is closed
explanation: Punctures can inoculate bacteria and damage deeper structures beneath a small skin opening.

stem: A patient is in respiratory arrest but has a pulse. What support may be needed under the CPR protocol?
options: Ventilation and airway support
Chest compressions alone
Fluids and a warming blanket
Atropine given IV
explanation: Respiratory arrest with circulation requires prompt ventilation and airway management.

stem: Ingestion of Easter lily (Lilium) pollen or leaves by a cat can cause:
options: Cardiac arrhythmia only
Seizures from hypoglycemia
Acute kidney injury
Liver failure without kidney involvement
explanation: All parts of true lilies (Lilium) and daylilies (Hemerocallis), even pollen or vase water, can cause kidney failure in cats. Early decontamination and IV fluids are critical.

stem: Grapiprant (Galliprant) relieves osteoarthritis pain in dogs by:
options: Blocking both COX enzymes completely
Acting on mu-opioid receptors
Binding nerve growth factor
Blocking the EP4 prostaglandin receptor
explanation: Grapiprant is a piprant that blocks the EP4 receptor, which drives pain and inflammation, rather than blocking prostaglandin production.

stem: Which behavior may indicate pain in a rabbit?
options: Grinding teeth loudly and sitting stretched out
Increased grooming and frequent eating
Running laps and thumping the hind feet
Reduced appetite and decreased normal activity
explanation: Prey species may show subtle signs such as reduced appetite and activity.

stem: A cat hides and resists handling after a procedure. What should the technician consider?
options: That it is fully recovered and doesn't need monitoring
Pain or stress and reassess using a feline-appropriate approach
That it needs more sedation before it is handled
That it is angry and should be left for the day
explanation: Withdrawal and defensive behavior can indicate pain or fear and need assessment.

stem: Why is a validated pain scale useful?
options: It can be used to diagnose the cause of the pain
It supports consistent assessment and comparison over time
It removes the need for the veterinarian's judgment
It tells the team exactly which drug to give
explanation: Structured scales improve consistency but are interpreted with clinical context.

stem: Frunevetmab (Solensia) is used to control osteoarthritis pain in cats. What is it?
options: An anti-NGF antibody injection
A daily oral NSAID tablet
A transdermal opioid gel applied daily
A gabapentin liquid given twice daily
explanation: It binds nerve growth factor, a key driver of osteoarthritis pain. Bedinvetmab (Librela) is the canine version.

stem: Which sign may indicate acute pain in a dog?
options: Sleeping soundly and stretching normally
Eating well and greeting staff at the door
Wagging and seeking attention from staff
Guarding or flinching when an area is approached
explanation: Guarding and flinching can be behavioral signs of pain.

stem: Why should pain be assessed before and after an intervention?
options: To decide whether the client will need pain medication at home
To compare baseline with response to treatment
To confirm that the drug was given at the correct time
To see whether the patient is sedated enough to handle
explanation: Before-and-after assessment helps evaluate treatment effect.

stem: What is multimodal analgesia?
options: Using more than one approach or mechanism to manage pain
